title: Two things sampling does to sound
sub: Aliasing above the Nyquist frequency, and leakage from cutting a signal into frames.

frames.caption: A 3 Hz sine (grey), sampled 20 times a second (dots). The Nyquist limit is half the sample rate, 10 Hz. Below it, the samples pin down the sine uniquely: the smoothest curve through them (blue) is the original.
8 Hz: still below 10 Hz. Few samples per cycle, but enough to reconstruct it exactly.

12 Hz: above Nyquist. The samples are exactly the ones an 8 Hz sine would give, so a reconstruction recovers 8 Hz: the 12 Hz tone has been aliased to 20 − 12 = 8 Hz. Nothing after sampling can tell the two apart.
18 Hz shows up as 2 Hz. This is why audio is low-pass filtered before sampling, and why 16 kHz speech audio cannot represent anything above 8 kHz.

A 25 ms frame (400 samples at 16 kHz) containing a loud 1,010 Hz tone and a tone at 1,330 Hz that is 40 dB quieter. With a rectangular window (just cutting the frame out), the loud tone's energy leaks into every bin as sidelobes, falling off only slowly. The quiet tone is buried.

The Hann window tapers the frame to zero at both ends. Its main lobe is wider (slightly blurrier frequency), but its sidelobes start around −31 dB instead of −13 dB and fall off much faster. The quiet tone now stands out as its own peak at about −40 dB.
